```{r, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(knitr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    error = FALSE,
    tidy  = FALSE,
    warning = FALSE,
    message = FALSE,
    comment = NA,
    fig.align = "center")
library(argitect)

options(cli.num_colors = 1)

run_code = function(code_block, argv_str) {
    chunks = knitr:::knit_code$get()
    argitect_options("__argv_str__" = argv_str)
    local({ 
        for(cb in code_block)
            eval(parse(text = chunks[[cb]])) 
    })
    argitect_options(RESET = TRUE)
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------


**argitect** (a phonetic approximation of "architect") is a pure-R command-line argument parser. It reimplements
the functionality of the Perl module [**Getopt::Long**](https://metacpan.org/pod/Getopt::Long)
without any external dependency, and additionally supports positional
arguments and flexible help messages.

## A quick example


The following code is normally put to the beginning of an R script:

```{r simple, eval = FALSE}
library(argitect)

cutoff = 0.05
argitect(
    "number=i", "Number of items.",
    "cutoff=f", "Cutoff for filtering results.",
    "verbose!", "Print messages."
)
```

The script (if the script is called `foo.R`) is then executed with command-line arguments, for example in
one of the following forms:

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --number 4 --cutoff 0.01 --verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R --number=4 -cutoff=0.01 --verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R -n 4 -c 0.01 -v
~\> Rscript foo.R -n4 -c=0.01 -v
~\> Rscript foo.R -n=4 --no-verbose
```

In this example, `number` is a mandatory option and it should only be in integer
mode. `cutoff` is optional and it already has a default value 0.05. `verbose` is
a logical option. If parsing is successful, two variables `number` and `verbose`
will be imported into the working environment with the specified values.
Value for `cutoff` will be updated if it is specified in command-line.

The help message is automatically generated according to the option specifications.

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --help
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("simple", "--help")
```

## Specification

Each specifier of command-line options consists of two parts: the name
specification and the option specification.

```
length|size|l=i@{}
```

Here `length|size|l` is a list of option names separated by `|`, where
`length` is the main option name, and others are aliases. The remaining part
(`i@{}`) is the option specification which defines the data mode, the storage type, and
the range of the arguments.


```
[option name|alias name...]=[mode][type][constraint]
```

### The option name

In a specification, there is a main option name. Multiple alias names are allowed.
The main argument name must only contain letters, numbers, characters of
`_` or `.` (but cannot start with `_`). It must be a valid R object name. There is
no naming restriction for alias names. In the following example:

```
length|size=i
```

It can be specified as one of

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --length 12
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 12
```

both pointing to the `length` option. When partial matching from the first
character is unique, users can provide a part of the option name.

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --len 12
~\> Rscript foo.R --si 12
```

It does not matter whether the command-line argument is specified by `--` or `-`, or the
value is specified by a space or `=`.

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --length=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -length=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -len=12
~\> Rscript foo.R --size=12
```

If the first letter of the option name is unique, it can be used as a single-letter flag.

```
~\> Rscript foo.R -l 12
~\> Rscript foo.R -l=12
~\> Rscript foo.R -l12
```

Since the main option name does not allow the character of `"-"`, for multi-word option names,
underline can be used to connect words while in the command-line interface, hyphen can be used instead.
For example, for the following specification,

```
min_length_of_word=i
```

then under command-line, this option can be set via:

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --min-length-of-word 10
```

Of cource `--min_length_of_word 10` also works.

### Data mode

Four data modes are supported, which are logical, integer, numeric and character, encoded by a single-letter:

- `l`, logical,
- `i`, integer,
- `f`, numeric,
- `s`, character.

For the logical mode, `verbose=l` is the same as `verbose!`. The configuration of logical options will be
introduced in Section "Logical argument".

In particular, for the integer mode, besides providing a normal decimal integer as the option value
under the command-line, integers can also be in the binary, octal, and hexadecimal
forms.

```
num=i
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 20
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0b10100
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0o24     # or --num 024
~\> Rscript foo.R --num 0x14
```

### Where do the arguments go

Options with values from command-line arguments will be imported into an
environment as R variables. By default it is the environment where `argitect()` 
is called. The first name in the option name specification is taken as the
corresponding variable name. That is why we require the first option name to be a
valid R object. If the R variable is already defined with a proper value, the
corresponding option will have default value, and is then called an optional
option that not mandatory to be specified on the command-line.


```{r where, eval = FALSE}
cutoff = 0.05
argitect(
    "number=i", "Number of items.",
    "cutoff=f", "Cutoff for filtering results.",
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)

print(number)
print(cutoff)
print(verbose)
```

In this example, `cutoff` already has a default value `0.05`, then it is optional on the command-line.

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --number 2 --verbose
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("where", "--number 2 --verbose")
```

Note the format of the default value of an option should be compatible to the corresponding specification.
We will introduce it in later sections.

### Logical argument

A logical option always has a default value of `FALSE` if it is not created in advance.

```{r logical, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("logical", "--help")
```

`"verbose!"` and `"verbose=l"` are identical. A default value can also be set for logical option.

```{r logical2, eval = FALSE}
verbose = TRUE
argitect(
    "verbose!", "Print message."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("logical2", "--help")
```

The negation of a logical option can be specified as one of:

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --no-verbose
~\> Rscript foo.R --not-verbose
```

If a single letter flag is available for each logical option, they can be bundled to specify.

```{r bundling, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "close!",  "Close the connection.",
    "delete!", "Delete the file.",
    "exit!",   "Exit the script."
)
```


```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("bundling", "--help")
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R -cde
~\> Rscript foo.R -cd -e
```

Or manually set a single-letter name for each logical option:

```{r bundling2, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "close |a!",  "Close the connection.",
    "delete|b!",  "Delete the file.",
    "exit  |c!",  "Exit the script."
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
run_code("bundling2", "--help")
```


```
~\> Rscript foo.R -abc
```

If there is already an option `abc=i`, then `-abc` has the priority to match the `abc` option.


### Data storage type

There are three storage type of option values: a single scalar element, a vector-like object
and an object of name-value pairs. Each structure has a special mark symbol to represent.

#### Scalar

The symbol for the scalar data structure is `$`, however, it can be ommited because it is
the default symbol if not specified.

```
size=i$
size=i
```

Logical options also correspond to logical scalars, the specification is one of:

```
verbose=l
verbose!
```

A bare symbol of positinoal argument also returns a scalar.

```
pos=i#
```

If an option has a default value, the data mode and structure should be
compatible with the corresponding specification.


#### Vector

Technically, in R, a scalar is a vector of length 1. However, here we
discriminate these two scenarios. The symbol for vector/array is `@`, where a
set of values can be specified after the option name.


```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@", "Size of a cubic."
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3
```

A positional option explicitely with `{}` also accepts a set of values.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "rgb=i#{}", "RGB channels."
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R 255 10 10
```

`size=i@` and `size=i@{}` are identical. `{}` is used to put constraints
inside, which will be introduced in the next section.


#### Hash/List

<div> <p style="padding:9.5px;border:1px solid #FF0000;background-color:#FFEEEE;border-radius:4px;">
It is not proper to call it a hash
since the option is stored as an R list structure while not a hash. However, the
<b>argitect</b> package is developed based on the Perl module
<b>Getopt:Long</b> where <code>%</code> is the symbol for hash. So here we still call
it a hash to emphasize it contains name-value pairs.</p> </div>

The symbol for hash is `%`, where a list of name-value pairs are specified after the option name.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i%", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size a=1 b=2 c=3
```

`size=i%` and `size=i%{}` are identical.

### Option constraint

For the options in the structure of vectors and hashes, the amount of elements can be further controlled.


The number of values for `size` is between 2 and 4:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@{2,4}", "size"
)
```

The number of values for `size` does not exceed 3:


```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@{,3}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 
```

The number of values for `size` is at least 3:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@{3,}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3 4
```

A set of names can be set in `{}`, then the option will be a named vector. 
In the next example, `size` can only accept two elements.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@{foo,bar}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2
```

Then on the R environment, the value of `size` is `c(foo = 1L, bar = 2L)`.

Adding a tailing comma allows more self-defined names besides those having been provided.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i@{foo,bar,}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2 abs=3 xyz=4
```

Similarly for hash, the following example only allows two elements for `size`. 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i%{foo,bar}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2
```

The command-line usages is
the same as `i@{foo,bar}`, but here `size` has the value of `list(foo = 1L, bar = 2L)`.

Adding a tailing comma also allows more self-defined names.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i%{foo,bar,}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1 bar=2 abs=3 xyz=4
```

Being different from vectors, elements in a hash (or a list) can be in different
modes. The the data mode can be defined as `i%` which globally controls the
data mode of all its elements. Also data mode can be set for individual
elements.

In the next example, the global mode is integer `i`, sub-argument `foo` has its own mode `f` and `bar` inherits the global one.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i%{foo=f,bar}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1.5 bar=2
```

If the data mode is not specified on the global level, then every individual sub-argument should explicitely specify its data mode.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=f,bar=i}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1.5 bar=2
```

Besides sub-argument as scalars, they can also be vectors. In the next
example, sub-argument `foo` expects a set of integers. For the list of
values assign to a sub-argument, elements should be separated by one of
`","`, `";"`, `":"`, `"|"` and `"/"` without spaces. 

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i@,bar=f}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1,2,3,4 bar=1.5
```

Similarly, constraints of sub-argument can be set as follows, but constraints as a set of names are not allowed for sub-arguments (only allows numeric constraints).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i@{2,3},bar=s@{1,2}}", "size"
)
```

Sub-argument allows alias names. There is no restriction of how to name them.


```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i%{foo|bar|xyz", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1
~\> Rscript foo.R --size bar=1
~\> Rscript foo.R --size xyz=1
```

On the R side, the value of `size` is always `list(foo = 1L)`.


For positional options, one (e.g. `{3}`, `{3,}`, `{,3}`) or two numbers (`{2,4}`) can be used to specify the ranges of the number of values.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i#{3}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 3
```

In the positional option specification, names are also allowed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "rgb=i#{red, green, blue}", "RGB channels."
)
```


```
~\> Rscript foo.R 255 128 128
```

In above example, `rgb` is stored as `c(red = 255L, green = 128L, blue = 128L)`. Note positional option does not allow tailing comma.

Positional options can also be put as sub-arguments. Following are examples:


```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i#, bar=s}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 bar=a
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i#{2}, bar=s@}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 bar=a,b,c
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1,2 bar=a,b,c
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1,2 bar=a,b,c
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i#{2}, bar=s#{}}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 a b c
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1,2 a,b,c
~\> Rscript foo.R --size foo=1,2 bar=a,b,c
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=%{foo=i#{2}, bar=i#{3}}", "size"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1 2 4 5 6
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 1,2 4,5,6
```

Then `size` has the value `list(foo = 1:2, bar = 4:5)`.

### Positional options

Positional options can be put as the first few options or the last few options in the specification.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "size=i", "Size.",
    "cutoff=c", "Cutoff.",
    "file=s#", "File"
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R --size 10 --cutoff 0.01 input.txt
```

Or

```{r, eval = FALSE}
argitect(
    "file=s#", "File"，
    "size=i", "Size.",
    "cutoff=c", "Cutoff."
)
```

```
~\> Rscript foo.R input.txt --size 10 --cutoff 0.01 
```
